To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the bare voice sentences are not derived from the morphological voice sentences by a simple rule of movement, (ii) the bare voices do not have a passive interpretation, (iii) the bare voice is not a “pseudo-passive,” (iv) bare voice sentences are derived from morphological voice sentences, (v) the morphological voice is not the “primary” or “genuine” voice and the bare voice is the “secondary” or “pseudo” voice.

(i) the bare passive is not an “imperfect passive,” but rather a true passive; (ii) there is no evidence that the bare passive has an “ergative” reading; and (iii) the bare passive and the morphological passive are not in a “competition,” but rather they are complementary.
the morphological and bare voices are used to mark the same semantic voice distinction, but they do so in different ways.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the optionality of morphological and bare voices is made sense of by Malay/Indonesians.
the following questions: (1) What are the syntactic, semantic and pragmatic differences between the morphological and the bare voices?
the optionality of morphological and bare voice marking and how this optionality is regulated by discourse factors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the bare voices are used for first and/or second person agents, whereas morphological voices are preferred for third person agents.
there are two voices in Malay/Indonesia, namely morphological and bare voice.
the two voices are in complementary distribution, with the morphological passive being used when the agent is not the speaker or the addressee, and with the bare passive being used when it is.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the two voices are not just two different types of passives, but two distinct constructions with different properties.

the bare voices have the same semantic properties as their morphological counterparts, and the bare active and passive are used in the same way as their morphologically marked counterparts, except that they are used for first and/or second person agents, which is not possible with their morphological counterparts.
the bare voices are “genuinely” active or passive, and the morphological voices are not.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the two sets of voices are in complementary distribution and that the bare voices do not have a passive function.
the two types of marking are not two different voices but two different ways of marking the same voice.
the optionality of the morphological voices in Malay/Indonesia is a result of the interplay between two factors: the morphological voice system itself and discourse factors.
